text: Three reviews cover emerging biotechnologies. Nanotechnologies—magnetic nanoparticles, quantum dots, carbon nanotubes, polyplexes and engineered nanoscale scaffolds—enable stem cell labeling, in vivo tracking, intracellular gene/protein delivery, differentiation and transplantation, though cytotoxicity remains a concern. Optogenetics provides high-temporal-precision in vivo control via light; applying molecular trafficking principles expands its repertoire: optical regulation at the far-red/infrared border and across the visible spectrum, stronger inhibition without higher light power (nanoampere-scale chloride photocurrents with reversible, step-like kinetics), and cell targeting by genetic identity, morphology and tissue topology—valuable where promoters are unknown or organisms genetically intractable. DNA methylation, a "silencing" epigenetic mark of 5-methylcytosine proposed in the 1970s, is now mapped genome-wide. Its function varies by context—transcriptional start sites with or without CpG islands, gene bodies, regulatory elements and repeats—and its link to transcription is more nuanced than first realized, essential for interpreting disease-associated changes such as cancer.
